clue.text: Pay jailed criminal to strangle knight and Lilith's architect

indicators.note: to strangle is to grip round the neck, so the scrambled letters close round the knight's letter
criminal means bent or crooked, so the letters of these two words are bent into a new order

parts.note: N is the chess notation for a knight

explanation.surface: Someone bribes a jailed criminal to throttle a knight and a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'criminal' rearranges PAY JAILED into JEAPLAIDY, and 'to strangle' wraps it round N to give JEAN PLAIDY.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean Plaidy, the pen name of Eleanor Hibbert, wrote the historical novel Lilith, so she built that book.

clue.text: Chap who did Absalom Absalom!'s introduction in writing, say

indicators.note: in tells us the opening letter is placed inside the example of writing

parts.note: the Book of Job is one example of a piece of scripture or writing

indicators.note: an introduction is the opening, so only the first letter of Absalom is taken

explanation.surface: It seems to ask who wrote the opening of Faulkner's novel Absalom, Absalom!
explanation.walkthrough: Faulkner's title points to literature, but 'did' means killed: in the Bible, King David's general Joab killed the rebel prince Absalom.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Second Book of Samuel the commander Joab put the rebellious prince Absalom to death, so he 'did' him in.

clue.text: Barmaids regularly avoided the guy who built The Green Man

definitions.text: the guy who built The Green Man

indicators.note: regularly avoided says every other letter of barmaids is skipped, leaving the alternate ones

explanation.surface: A pub owner who kept away from the barmaids sounds like the landlord of a pub called The Green Man.
explanation.walkthrough: The Green Man sounds like a pub, which goes well with barmaids, but here it is Kingsley Amis's 1969 ghost novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Kingsley Amis wrote the novel The Green Man, so he is its builder in the literary sense.

clue.text: Around noon, compatriots dashed after Byron and his ilk

indicators.note: Around says the scrambled word goes round the letter for noon
dashed means smashed or wrecked, so the letters of compatriots are broken up and reordered

parts.note: N stands for noon, as on a clock or in timetables

explanation.surface: Fellow countrymen rush off at midday to follow Lord Byron and poets like him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dashed' rearranges COMPATRIOTS, and 'Around' puts that round N to give POSTROMANTIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Byron belongs to the Romantic movement, so whatever follows that era and its poets is post-Romantic.

clue.text: A Helmer is one to knock back a basket case's brother

indicators.note: to knock back is to push backwards, so the heroine's name is read in reverse

parts.note: Nora Helmer is the heroine of Ibsen's play A Doll's House

explanation.surface: It seems to describe someone rejecting a person who is a nervous wreck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to knock back' reverses NORA to ARON. A 'basket case' looks like a wreck, but it is the baby Moses, left in a basket among the bulrushes.
explanation.definitionFit: In Exodus Aaron is the elder brother of Moses, who as an infant was hidden in a basket on the Nile.

clue.text: "From heat to heat the day -, / And slowly rounded to the east" (Tennyson)

definitions.text: "From heat to heat the day -, / And slowly rounded to the east" (Tennyson)

parts.words: From heat to heat the day -, / And slowly rounded to the east
parts.note: a gap-fill quotation from Tennyson's In Memoriam: the missing verb says the daylight grew less

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: the missing past-tense verb tells how the day diminished as evening came.
explanation.definitionFit: The line describes the daylight lessening and dwindling as the sun went down.

clue.text: What Renton took is, around about, sixteen grand primarily

indicators.note: around says the two picked letters sit on either side of the abbreviation
primarily means at first, so the first letters of sixteen and grand are taken

parts.note: CA, short for circa, means about

explanation.surface: It seems to price the drugs Mark Renton bought at roughly sixteen thousand pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark Renton is the heroin-addicted narrator of Irvine Welsh's Trainspotting.
explanation.definitionFit: Scag is slang for heroin, the drug Renton is hooked on in Trainspotting.

clue.text: Fishy work requires new Carry On cast

indicators.note: cast means thrown about, so these letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: It sounds as if a smelly job needs a fresh line-up of Carry On film actors.
explanation.walkthrough: Carry On is a series of British comedy films, and 'cast' looks like their actors, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Steinbeck's novel Cannery Row is set among sardine-canning plants in Monterey, so the book smells of fish.

clue.text: Keller's work affected her energy around November

indicators.note: around says the rearranged letters wrap round the letter for November
affected means altered, so the letters of her energy are changed into a new order

parts.note: N is November in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Helen Keller's achievement was something that had an effect on her energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'affected' rearranges HER ENERGY into GREEHENRY, and 'around' puts that round N. Keller is the Swiss writer Gottfried Keller, not Helen Keller.
explanation.definitionFit: Gottfried Keller's novel Der grüne Heinrich is known in English by this title.

clue.text: A girl mixed up with a case that details Kinnear's killing

indicators.note: mixed up means jumbled together, so the letters of these words are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: A young woman gets entangled in a legal case about a murder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixed up' rearranges A GIRL and A CASE together, with 'with' just joining the two.
explanation.definitionFit: Margaret Atwood's novel Alias Grace retells the 1843 murder of Thomas Kinnear and his housekeeper in Canada.

clue.text: Rice and noodles non-combatants eat at the front

indicators.note: at the front tells us to take the first letter of each of the following words

explanation.surface: It reads like a scene of civilians eating rice and noodles while troops fight.
explanation.walkthrough: Rice is not the food but the American novelist Anne Rice, author of Interview with the Vampire.
explanation.definitionFit: Anne Rice was the gothic novelist, so her forename stands in for her surname here.

clue.text: Book series by a talented young man

indicators.note: by means beside, so the article stands next to the word for series

parts.note: a suit is a set or series, as in a suit of cards
able means talented or skilful
a boy is a young man

explanation.surface: It looks like a set of novels written by a gifted youth.
explanation.definitionFit: A Suitable Boy is Vikram Seth's long novel, so it is a book in its own right.

clue.text: Doctor direct with nurse who put words in Alice's mouth

parts.note: frank means direct or candid
EN is short for Enrolled Nurse

parts.words: who put words in Alice's mouth
parts.note: Gertrude Stein wrote The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas, telling her own life in her partner's voice

explanation.surface: A doctor works closely with a nurse who scripted what a girl named Alice said.
explanation.walkthrough: Alice suggests Lewis Carroll, but it is Alice B. Toklas, whose 'autobiography' was really written by Gertrude Stein.
explanation.definitionFit: Victor Frankenstein, Mary Shelley's scientist, is often called Doctor Frankenstein.

clue.text: I knocked out The Wild Knight and box heavyweight around ears on occasion

definitions.text: I knocked out The Wild Knight

indicators.note: around says the two words together surround the letters from ears

parts.note: a chest is a box
a ton is a heavy weight

indicators.note: on occasion means now and then, so only alternate letters of ears are used

explanation.surface: A boxer boasts of flattening a wild knight, with a heavyweight punching about the ears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocked out' is boxing language that fits 'box' and 'heavyweight', but here it means wrote quickly; 'I' is the poet speaking about his own book.
explanation.definitionFit: G. K. Chesterton's first poetry collection was The Wild Knight and Other Poems, which he dashed off in his twenties.

clue.text: Work planned by London high-flyer and former PM

parts.note: a martin is a swallow-like bird that flies high
Anthony Eden was the British Prime Minister from 1955 to 1957

explanation.surface: A building project in London designed by a high achiever and an ex-prime minister.
explanation.walkthrough: London is not the city but the American writer Jack London.
explanation.definitionFit: Martin Eden is a 1909 novel by Jack London, so it was a work he devised.

clue.text: Characteristics of folk like Twain: brains primarily

indicators.note: primarily means first, so the word for brains comes before the other piece

parts.note: the head is where the brains are, so head stands for brains
Mark Twain shares his forename with others called Mark, so folk like him are Marks

explanation.surface: It claims that intelligence is what marks out writers like Mark Twain.
explanation.definitionFit: Headmarks is an old word for the distinguishing features or traits of a person.

clue.text: Describe again energy-filled King Lear's head in mental distress

indicators.note: filled says the word for king has the energy letter put inside it

parts.note: Rex is Latin for king
E is the physics symbol for energy

indicators.note: in says the leading letter is placed inside the word for mental distress

parts.note: pain can mean mental suffering or anguish

indicators.note: head means the first letter of Lear's

explanation.surface: King Lear, half mad and full of energy, tries to tell his story again.
explanation.definitionFit: To re-explain is to set something out once more so that it is understood.

clue.text: Conductor or keyboardist's admission?

definitions.meaning: an intrinsic semiconductor, made from pure silicon or germanium
a typist owning up to the job would say the two words '...'

explanation.surface: It asks whether a music director or a keyboard player is confessing something.
explanation.walkthrough: Conductor and keyboardist suggest music; the first is electrical and the second a typist.
explanation.definitionFit: A pure semiconductor is described as intrinsic, or I-type; and a typist would say of their work 'I type'.

clue.text: Cigar-smoking ragamuffin in group doctor brought back

annotationWithheld.why: Cigar-smoking ragamuffin in group doctor brought back (5): SET + reversed NO would give the letters, but no source confirms who the cigar-smoking ragamuffin called Seton is, so the definition cannot be explained honestly
annotationWithheld.clue: Cigar-smoking ragamuffin in group doctor brought back

clue.text: Morse over Auden … ridiculous

indicators.note: ridiculous means absurd, so the letters of these words are rearranged into something absurd-looking

explanation.surface: A detective named Morse is preferred to the poet Auden, which seems ridiculous.
explanation.walkthrough: Endeavour is Inspector Morse's rarely used first name, in Colin Dexter's novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Colin Dexter's detective Inspector Morse turned out to have the forename Endeavour.

clue.text: European in XL pants is a Pulitzer-prize winner

annotationWithheld.why: European in XL pants is a Pulitzer-prize winner (1,5,6): E for European is clear, but no reading of 'in XL pants is a' gives ANNIEPROULX (the letters O, R, U are not there to rearrange), and no source gives the parse
annotationWithheld.clue: European in XL pants is a Pulitzer-prize winner

clue.text: Old publication first seen in Hampshire town

parts.note: a mag, short for magazine, is a publication

indicators.note: first seen in says only the opening letter of Hampshire is used

explanation.surface: An old magazine first turned up in a town in Hampshire, a county in southern England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hampshire town' looks like the definition, but Omagh is in Northern Ireland: Hampshire gives only its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Omagh is the county town of Tyrone in Northern Ireland.

clue.text: Family novel ultimately set in American jail

indicators.note: set in says the final letter is placed inside the slang word for jail

parts.note: can is American slang for prison

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so the last letter of novel is taken

explanation.surface: A family saga set in an American prison.
explanation.definitionFit: A clan is an extended family group, especially in the Scottish Highlands.

clue.text: Headers from notably awful striker hilarious, amusing linesman

indicators.note: headers are the heads or first letters, so one is taken from each of the next four words

explanation.surface: A football report: a dreadful striker's headers were laughable, and the linesman found it funny.
explanation.walkthrough: Football terms throughout: 'headers' and 'linesman' suggest the pitch, but the linesman writes lines of verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Ogden Nash was an American writer of comic verse, a writer of funny lines.

clue.text: Part of haircut oddly-shorn? Bloody barber!

indicators.note: Part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone shouts at a barber who has given them a badly cut haircut.
explanation.walkthrough: Sweeney Todd is the murderous barber of Fleet Street; 'Bloody' looks like a British swear word but means bloodstained.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweeney Todd, the demon barber of Victorian melodrama, cut his customers' throats.

clue.text: Cossack dancing bar a blast, you must go in there

indicators.note: must go in there says the letter for you is placed inside the rearranged letters
dancing means moving about, so the letters of these words move into a new order

parts.note: U sounds like you, as in text speak

explanation.surface: Cossacks dancing in a bar are great fun, and you should join in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dancing' rearranges BAR A BLAST into TARASBLBA, and U goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Taras Bulba is Gogol's novella about an old Zaporozhian Cossack leader.

clue.text: French Tart and fruit graduate polished off

indicators.note: polished off means finished or removed, so the degree letters are taken out of the fruit

parts.note: a banana is a fruit
BA, Bachelor of Arts, is a graduate

explanation.surface: A French pastry and fruit are eaten up by a student.
explanation.walkthrough: A French tart looks like a pastry, but it is a courtesan: Zola's novel Nana is about one.
explanation.definitionFit: Nana, the heroine of Zola's novel, is a Parisian courtesan, so a French woman of easy virtue.

clue.text: "Than angels. Cease to wail and brawl! / Why — to darkness crawl?" (Tennyson)

definitions.text: "Than angels. Cease to wail and brawl! / Why — to darkness crawl?" (Tennyson)

parts.words: Than angels. Cease to wail and brawl! / Why — to darkness crawl?
parts.note: a gap-fill quotation from Tennyson: the missing phrase says how slowly and gradually one creeps toward the dark

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: the missing words describe crawling little by little.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means gradually, by very small steps, which suits a slow crawl.
